name: Manka Longshan Temple
address: No. 211, Guangzhou St, Wanhua District, Taipei City
description: In the front hall (the Sanchuan Hall) of Manka Longshan Temple stands a pair of cast-bronze dragon pillars, the first bronze dragon pillars ever used in Taiwan, installed during the 1919 rebuilding. This is one of the oldest temples in Taipei's Wanhua District, and even the columns holding up its roof have a story. Walk through the three halls, laid out around courtyards like the character 回, and look up: the caisson ceiling is carved in a spiral, ring after ring narrowing upward in astonishing detail. Longshan Temple is dedicated first to Guanyin Bodhisattva, but its rear and side halls house more than a hundred other deities, among them Mazu, Wenchang Dijun, Lord Guan (Guansheng Dijun) and Yue Lao, the Old Man Under the Moon. One temple holds the whole Taiwanese habit of praying to gods and buddhas side by side: people come for exam success, for love, for safety, each at the right altar. International visitors flock here, yet to the people of Wanhua it is simply the temple where they burn incense on the 1st and 15th of the lunar month. Stone carving, woodwork and painted decoration fill every corner, and when worship peaks the whole forecourt is packed with people.
history: In 1738, the third year of the Qing Qianlong reign, a group of immigrants from the Three Districts of Quanzhou crossed the strait and brought a divided spirit of Guanyin from the Longshan Temple in their hometown of Jinjiang to Manka, where they built this temple. In its early years it was more than a place to pray. It was where the immigrants met and settled community affairs, and during the Qing-era clan clash known as the Ding-Xia Jiao Feud it became a scene of history itself. Over the next two centuries and more, earthquakes, storms and war came again and again. The closest call came at the end of World War II, when an Allied air raid destroyed the main hall completely, yet the principal Guanyin statue survived. Devotees still tell this as Longshan Temple's greatest miracle. The temple's overall layout today comes from the rebuilding that began in 1919, designed by the master craftsman Wang Yi-shun; the main hall bombed in 1945 was rebuilt between 1953 and 1959. Reborn from disaster, this old temple has become a landmark of traditional Taiwanese temple architecture, and in 2018 it was raised to the status of a National Monument.

visit.gettingThere: MRT Bannan (Blue) Line to Longshan Temple Station, then about a 3-minute walk. If you drive, park at the Monga Park underground garage across the street.
visit.whenToGo: The temple is busiest on the 1st and 15th of every lunar month, and on Guanyin's three feast days (lunar 2/19, 6/19, and 9/19).

name: Xingtian Temple
address: No. 109, Minquan E. Rd. Sec. 2, Zhongshan District, Taipei City
description: Xingtian Temple has never burned joss paper. In 2014 this Enzhugong temple in Taipei's Zhongshan District went further and removed the great incense burner from its forecourt, encouraging worshippers to pray with their palms pressed together instead. It is dedicated to Lord Guan (Guansheng Dijun), yet it goes against the usual temple grain: there is no donation box and no animal offerings, only a focus on sincerity of heart and honest reflection. The building is grand in scale but almost bare of elaborate carving, which only makes it feel more solemn. What people remember most are the volunteers in sky-blue robes. When their minds are unsettled or their luck is low, many come here and wait in line for these volunteers to perform shoujing, a ritual to calm a frightened spirit, hoping to leave with a little peace of body and mind.
history: Xingtian Temple's story begins with a lay devotee named Huang Chong, whom worshippers honor as Master Xuankong. Vowing to serve Lord Guan, he first founded Xingtian Hall in 1943, and the temple at its present site was completed in 1968. Next to many centuries-old shrines, Xingtian Temple is young, yet it quickly became one of the busiest places of worship in northern Taiwan. Master Xuankong set down rules meant to encourage goodness: no donation box, no animal offerings, no burning of joss paper. He passed away in 1970. In 2014, Xingtian Temple removed the great incense burner and offering tables from its forecourt, and its move to cut back on incense led other temples to follow. As for the shoujing service known across Taiwan, it still draws crowds of worshippers every day and remains the most vivid part of daily life at Xingtian Temple.

name: Dalongdong Baoan Temple
address: No. 61, Hami St, Datong District, Taipei City
description: A temple can win international recognition for how well it is restored, and Dalongdong Baoan Temple did exactly that. Because its restoration held to traditional craftsmanship instead of taking modern shortcuts, this old temple in Taipei's Datong District received an Honourable Mention in the UNESCO Asia-Pacific Awards for Cultural Heritage Conservation in 2003, and it has become a model for temple restoration in Taiwan. It is dedicated to Baosheng Dadi, the god of medicine. Inside, the walls carry murals by the master painter Pan Li-shui, alongside fine koji pottery and woodcarving. With less of the usual temple bustle and more of a scholarly calm, stepping in feels like entering a quiet hall of art.
history: In 1742, the seventh year of the Qing Qianlong reign, immigrants from Tong'an brought a divided spirit of Baosheng Dadi from the Ciji Temple at Baijiao, in Quanzhou Prefecture, Fujian, to Dalongdong. As Dalongdong prospered, the temple grew with it. Fundraising for a large three-hall temple began in 1805, and the work was finally finished in 1830, setting the layout seen today. What truly made Baoan Temple famous was the great seven-year restoration from 1995 to 2002. The temple insisted on traditional methods, repairing it slowly brick by brick and tile by tile, and the result earned an Honourable Mention in the UNESCO Asia-Pacific Awards for Cultural Heritage Conservation in 2003. Every year the Baosheng Cultural Festival also features the fire lion ritual, using flames to drive away evil and pray for blessings, a rare and precious piece of folk tradition.

name: Taipei Xia-Hai City God Temple
address: No. 61, Dihua St. Sec. 1, Datong District, Taipei City
description: Tucked into Dihua Street in Taipei's Dadaocheng, Taipei Xia-Hai City God Temple covers only about 46 ping (a traditional Taiwanese unit of floor area), yet its incense never dies down. Its main deity is the City God who protects the neighborhood, but what really brings young people here in lines is Yue Lao, the Old Man Under the Moon. According to the temple's own count, more than 6000 couples come back each year to thank him, which has turned this small temple into a famous place to pray for love. After you pray, don't rush off: have a cup of the temple's peace tea for a wish of safety and a happy ending.
history: In 1856, the sixth year of the Qing Xianfeng reign, a group of Tong'an people in Dadaocheng pooled their money to build this City God temple to keep their neighborhood safe. It was the era when Dadaocheng was taking off on the tea trade, and the temple naturally became the spiritual center of the Tong'an merchants. The real turning point came in 1971, when the temple began enshrining Yue Lao. Wave after wave of people seeking love poured in, and this temple of about 46 ping became one of the most popular Yue Lao temples in all of Taiwan. Every year on the 13th day of the 5th lunar month, the Taipei City God procession draws such crowds that people call it "the 13th of the 5th month, when people watch people." For a hundred years it has remained one of Taipei's three great temple festivals.

name: Songshan Ciyou Temple
address: No. 761, Bade Rd. Sec. 4, Songshan District, Taipei City
description: Finish praying to Mazu, turn around, and you are at one of Taiwan's liveliest night markets. This is Songshan Ciyou Temple, popularly called the Songshan Mazu Temple, standing beside Raohe Street Night Market in Taipei's Songshan District and a classic example of Taiwan's temple-front culture. The main hall has a triple-eave roof, and the rear hall rises six stories high, glowing brilliantly once the lights come on at night. Its main deity is the black-faced Mazu, known for her compassion and answered prayers, and the temple also hosts Zhusheng Niangniang, the Tiger Lord and other deities. Light your incense, make your wish, then step straight into Raohe Night Market next door to eat your way through it. In one visit you walk through both everyday Taiwanese life and its folk faith.
history: In 1753, the eighteenth year of the Qing Qianlong reign, a wandering monk named Lin Shou-yi traveled about collecting donations and built Ciyou Temple. Songshan was still called Xikou then, an important transfer port on the Keelung River, and the temple became the shared center of faith for the residents of thirteen villages and streets. Under Japanese rule, Ciyou Temple was renovated twice, in 1915 and 1937. After the war, in 1981, a fire struck the main hall and it was rebuilt, the temple growing ever grander. From river port to railway stop to today's modern business district, Xikou has changed many times over, and Ciyou Temple has watched it all. Even now, the spot in front of the temple known as Ciyou Temple Entrance is the landmark Songshan locals know best in their daily lives.

name: Zhinan Temple
address: No. 115, Wanshou Rd, Wenshan District, Taipei City
description: "Couples who visit Zhinan Temple together will break up." That is the most widely told urban legend about this Xiangong Temple on the slopes of Mount Zhinan in Muzha, Taipei's Wenshan District. Zhinan Temple has long been called "the most sacred mountain under heaven." It is a well-known Taoist holy site in Taiwan, and also one of the rare temples that brings Confucianism, Taoism and Buddhism together. Built into the mountainside on a grand scale, it lets you look out over the whole Taipei Basin from in front of its halls. From the Chunyang Hall honoring Lü Dongbin (Lüzu) and the Lingxiao Hall of the Jade Emperor to the Mahavira Hall and the Dacheng Hall, it gathers immortals, buddhas and sages on the same mountain. As for the breakup legend, worshippers have since turned it around: the temple is now sought out for cutting off bad romantic ties and praying for the right partner, and people who want to clear up their love lives and start over climb the mountain on purpose to pray here.
history: In 1882, the eighth year of the Qing Guangxu reign, Wang Bin-lin, an assistant county magistrate in Manka, brought the incense of Lü Dongbin (Lüzu) to Taiwan; in 1890, local people built a temple on the present site. It was expanded generation after generation: the Lingxiao Hall was built from 1963 to 1966, and the Mahavira Hall (Buddhist) and the Dacheng Hall (Confucian) were completed one after another after the war, gradually growing into today's grand complex uniting Confucianism, Buddhism and Taoism. Zhinan Temple sits high on the mountain, and the climb up runs along more than a thousand stone steps under towering old trees, which is how it earned the name "the most sacred mountain under heaven." As for the popular saying that Lü Dongbin is strict about romance and will split up couples who visit together, it is groundless, yet by a twist of fate it has become the best-known anecdote about Zhinan Temple.

name: Hongludi Nanshan Fude Temple
address: No. 160-1, Ln. 399, Sec. 2, Xingnan Rd, Zhonghe District, New Taipei City
description: A statue of the Earth God, 108 tai-chi tall (traditional Taiwanese feet) including its base, stands on the hilltop looking down over all of Zhonghe. This is Hongludi Nanshan Fude Temple, one of northern Taiwan's best-known places to pray for wealth and the most eye-catching landmark in New Taipei's Zhonghe District. The giant Tudigong has a kindly face and holds a gold ingot steady in his hand. The temple sits on Nanshijiao Mountain with a wide-open view, so you can take in the night lights of greater Taipei on the same trip. It is open 24 hours, and the later it gets the busier it becomes: many salespeople and business owners like to come up at night to exchange for "mother money" and touch the gold ingot, praying for their fortunes to flow.
history: Faith in the Earth God at Hongludi began more than a century ago with a small shrine built on the mountain by tea farmers. It was rebuilt in 1952 and expanded between 1967 and 1971, reaching the scale it has today. One explanation of the name Hongludi, "stove land," is that the mountain's shape resembles a stove in feng shui terms, and feng shui masters have praised it as a rare spot that gathers wealth. That is exactly why Hongludi Nanshan Fude Temple became northern Taiwan's famous Earth God temple for praying for wealth. Around the end and start of each year, and on the Earth God's birthday on the 2nd day of the 2nd lunar month, the stream of people and cars heading up the mountain never stops. The giant Earth God statue on the summit, holding his gold ingot, has long been a landmark of Zhonghe with its gentle expression. After dark, looking down from the heights over the glittering lights of the Taipei Basin, it is no surprise that this has also become a famous night-view spot.

name: Taipei Confucius Temple
address: No. 275, Dalong St., Datong Dist., Taipei City
description: In the Dacheng Hall of Taipei Confucius Temple, you will not find a single statue. This Confucius temple in Taipei's Datong District follows the Confucian teaching of not worshipping idols, so the hall honors Confucius, the Supreme Sage and Foremost Teacher, with spirit tablets alone. Built in the Minnan style, every brick and pillar feels upright and solemn. The best reason to make a special trip is the ceremony honoring Confucius (the Shidian rite) held every year on Teachers' Day, September 28. By custom the mayor serves as chief officiant, young performers dance the ancient yi dance, and Confucius is honored with ancient rites. It is one of Taipei's most important celebrations of Confucian culture.
history: Taipei's first Confucius temple (Wen Temple) began construction in 1880, the sixth year of the Qing Guangxu reign, and was completed in 1884. Sadly, it was torn down in 1907, during Japanese rule. The temple you see today was rebuilt at the initiative of Taipei's local gentry in 1925. They brought in Wang Yi-shun, the master craftsman from Quanzhou who had designed Longshan Temple, and the work was not completed until 1939. It too is built in the Minnan style, and it pairs beautifully with Dalongdong Baoan Temple just across Dalong Street. One Confucian and one Taoist, the two buildings together form a cluster of traditional architecture in Dalongdong.

name: Taipei Wenchang Temple
address: No. 9, Ln. 45, Minsheng W. Rd., Zhongshan Dist., Taipei City
description: Every exam season, the walls of Taipei Wenchang Temple fill up with photocopies of exam admission tickets, layered so thickly that they become a sight in their own right. Standing beside Shuanglian MRT Station in Taipei's Zhongshan District, this is a well-known Wenchang temple in central Taipei, dedicated to Wenchang Dijun, the god in charge of scholarly success. Worshippers arrive carrying bags of punning offerings: scallions for cleverness, celery for diligence, radish (caitou) for good fortune, and zongzi rice dumplings, whose name sounds like "sure to pass." All their hopes of seeing their names on the pass list are placed in these offerings they can hold in their hands.
history: Taipei Wenchang Temple's origins go back to the Japanese era. It is said that a statue of Wenchang Dijun brought over by a merchant was left in the woods at Shuanglian, and was later found and enshrined; it was expanded in 1960. Later, because of construction on the MRT Tamsui Line, the temple moved into Minxiang Park and was rebuilt inside the park in 1992. It is not large, but its location in the heart of Taipei, its easy access and its long reputation for answered prayers gradually made it a temple students visit often. On the eve of every major exam, crowds of students and parents pour in to pray for good results, and the wall covered in admission tickets has become a unique cultural sight.

name: Songshan Fengtian Temple
address: No. 12, Ln. 221, Fude St., Xinyi Dist., Taipei City
description: At midnight as the 9th day of the first lunar month begins, Songshan Fengtian Temple is packed solid with worshippers who have come to honor Tiangong, the Lord of Heaven. It is the biggest night of the year. This Taoist temple in Taipei's Xinyi District is dedicated to Tiangong, the Jade Emperor, and is one of the most important centers of Jade Emperor worship in the Taipei area. The resplendent main hall enshrines the Jade Emperor, with the Three Officials (Sanguan Dadi) worshipped alongside him. If you want to see how Taiwanese people honor heaven with their most solemn rites, Tiangong's birthday on the 9th day of the first lunar month is the grandest lesson there is; the media call this the largest Tiangong temple in northern Taiwan.
history: Legend traces the prehistory of Fengtian Temple back to an incense burner in a stone cave on Tiger Mountain in 1862. In 1953, Songshan gentry including Wen Jin-bo and Liu Yong-hao pooled funds to put up a bamboo hut and formally named it Fengtian Temple. Worshippers grew in number year after year, and the temple was expanded again and again, with the Jade Emperor enshrined in the main hall. The incense in its Tiangong burner has never stopped burning strong, above all on Tiangong's birthday, the 9th day of the first lunar month, when worshippers begin pouring in at midnight to honor the Lord of Heaven. As Xinyi District kept developing and the crowds kept growing, Songshan Fengtian Temple became one of the most important centers of Jade Emperor worship in the Taipei area.

name: Keelung Dianji Temple
address: No. 27-2, Ren 3rd Rd, Ren'ai District, Keelung City
description: One of Taiwan's most famous night markets grows right around a temple, and that is the remarkable sight at Keelung Dianji Temple. Located in Keelung's Ren'ai District, it is one of Keelung's three great temples and is dedicated to Kaizhang Shengwang, the Sacred King Who Opened Zhangzhou. The whole Keelung Miaokou Night Market spreads outward with the temple at its center, creating a scene where the night market sits inside the temple grounds and wraps around the temple. It is both a center of faith and a food hub known across Taiwan, with incense and crowds that never fade all year. Look up at the carved beams and painted rafters inside, too; don't spend all your time eating.
history: In 1875, the first year of the Qing Guangxu reign, the Lin Ben Yuan family of Banqiao donated land to help build Dianji Temple, dedicated to Kaizhang Shengwang, and it became the most important center of faith for the Zhangzhou people of the Keelung area. Dianji Temple was damaged in the Yiwei War of 1895, repaired in 1897, and renovated again after the war between 1957 and 1964. All along, its fate was tied closely to Keelung's: from a Qing-era treaty port to the international harbor it later became, the temple watched over every boom and change of Keelung Harbor. The temple still keeps stone pillars from the Tongzhi era and the "Kai Min Di Yi" stele, recording the pioneering stories of Keelung's early settlers. And the Miaokou Night Market around the temple has long been Keelung's most iconic tourist landmark.

name: Hsinchu City God Temple
address: No. 75, Zhongshan Rd, North District, Hsinchu City
description: When it comes to divine rank, Hsinchu City God Temple is often called the highest-ranking City God temple in all of Taiwan. When it was elevated to the title of Duke Weiling in 1890, the sixteenth year of the Guangxu reign, it was granted a plaque reading "Jinmen Baozhang." This old temple in Hsinchu's North District draws a steady stream of worshippers, and its most powerful spectacle comes in the 7th lunar month during the Zhuqian Zhongyuan City God Festival. In the ritual of carrying the cangue to dissolve misfortune, thousands upon thousands of devotees parade through the streets wearing paper cangues in repentance, an awe-inspiring sight. After you pay your respects to the City God, don't miss the snacks around the temple square that are famous across Taiwan: meatball soup (gongwan), rice noodles and ba-wan, one stall after another. Here you can satisfy both faith and appetite in one visit.
history: In 1748, the thirteenth year of the Qing Qianlong reign, Zeng Ri-ying, the sub-prefect of Tamsui, proposed building Hsinchu City God Temple, and it is one of the oldest government-built temples in the Hsinchu area. In the Qing imagination, a City God temple was like a county yamen of the underworld. It faced the Hsinchu magistrate's yamen from afar, one serving the unseen world and one the living, a symbol of the idea that humans and gods govern together. It was repaired several times during the Jiaqing reign, and under Japanese rule the gentry member Zheng Zhao-ji led a large-scale renovation that set the layout seen today. The temple preserves a large number of Qing-dynasty plaques and couplets, the most famous being the "Li Yin Zan Yang" plaque inscribed by Zheng Yong-xi. The City God's procession through the district during the Zhongyuan season each year is a major religious event in Hsinchu City. The square in front of the temple and the stalls around it have also grown into the renowned City God Temple snack scene.

name: Taoyuan Jingfu Temple
address: No. 208, Zhongzheng Rd, Taoyuan District, Taoyuan City
description: When Taoyuan locals say they are going to "the Big Temple" to pray, they mean Jingfu Temple. This municipal monument in Taoyuan District, Taoyuan City, is the most important center of faith in the whole urban area. It is dedicated to Kaizhang Shengwang, the Sacred King Who Opened Zhangzhou, and was founded jointly by fifteen villages of Zhangzhou immigrants. Jingfu Temple has a distinctive roof style, a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof with false four-sided eaves, rising tier upon tier and making the exterior especially magnificent. It stands on the roundabout in the center of Taoyuan, a spiritual landmark that Taoyuan people can see just by looking up.
history: In 1745, the tenth year of the Qing Qianlong reign, the land reclamation leader Xue Qi-long donated fields to found the temple and enshrine Kaizhang Shengwang. In 1810, the fifteenth year of the Jiaqing reign, Jian Yue and others donated again to rebuild it, and when the work was completed in 1813 it was given the name Jingfu Temple. As Taoyuan developed, it became the most important center of faith in the city. In 1923 it was relocated because of urban redevelopment, with a design by the master craftsman Chen Ying-bin, and after the war it was renovated several times, in 1961, 1976, 1983 and 2006. From a Qing-era pioneer settlement to today's special municipality, Taoyuan has changed again and again, yet this Big Temple has always stood at the heart of the city, the shared spiritual stronghold of generation after generation of Taoyuan people.

name: Dharma Drum Mountain
address: No. 555, Fagu Rd., Jinshan Dist., New Taipei City
description: Step into Dharma Drum Mountain and you'll find it looks less like the incense-wreathed temple you might imagine and more like a serene mountain academy. This monastery set among the lush green hills of New Taipei's Jinshan District is one of Taiwan's four major Buddhist organizations, founded by Master Sheng Yen in 1989. Its architecture deliberately blends modern lines with the spirit of Zen, echoing everywhere the Master's ideal of 'protecting the spiritual environment.' The main hall enshrines Shakyamuni Buddha, and the campus also holds a meditation center and a Buddhist college. For anyone wishing to set the clamor aside for a while and learn to still the mind, Dharma Drum Mountain is the most representative place of Taiwanese Buddhism's modernization.
history: In 1989, Master Sheng Yen founded Dharma Drum Mountain in Jinshan, though the grand opening ceremony was not held until 2005. He put forward the ideal of 'uplifting the character of humanity and building a pure land on earth,' holding that Buddhism should not merely chant sutras deep in the mountains but step into society, care for the world, and purify the human heart. And so Dharma Drum Mountain is not only a Buddhist monastery but a comprehensive campus combining education, culture, and charity — a path that has earned it an important place in the international Buddhist community as well.

name: Beipu Citien Temple
address: No. 1, Beipu St, Beipu Township, Hsinchu County
description: The start of Beipu Old Street lies right on the stone-paved forecourt of Citien Temple. This county-designated historic site in Beipu Township, Hsinchu County, is the most representative Hakka center of faith in the whole county and the core landmark of the entire Beipu settlement. Dedicated to Guanyin Bodhisattva, it embodies the classic Hakka tradition of 'Guanyin first.' Its plan approaches the Cantonese-Hakka 'double-hall, two-wing' layout, and the Sanchuan Hall is distinguished by its sandstone carving; the pair of stone dragon pillars along the entrance colonnade are both carved as 'ascending dragons' coiling upward — a technique rarely seen in Taiwan's temples. Inside are also two sets of '24 Filial Exemplars' stone columns, finely carved and likewise rare across Taiwan. On weekends, follow the forecourt into the old street and the stream of visitors never stops.
history: The origins of Citien Temple are inseparable from the Han Chinese settlement of Beipu. In 1834, during the Daoguang reign, the Cantonese leader Jiang Xiuluan and the Hokkien merchant Zhou Bangzheng jointly formed the 'Jin Guang Fu' reclamation enterprise to open up the southeastern mountains of Hsinchu — and the Guanyin statue enshrined in the temple was, by tradition, personally brought back from mainland China by Jiang Xiuluan. In 1840 Jiang rebuilt it as a wooden temple. In 1874, during the Tongzhi reign, Jiang Xiuluan's eldest grandson Jiang Ronghua carried out another major reconstruction, adding two wings and a front hall and setting the 'two-hall, two-wing, two-side-house' layout of today. During the 'Beipu Incident' of 1907 in the late Guangxu period, Citien Temple even served as an important base, adding a page of far-reaching history to this temple.

name: Baozhong Yimin Temple
address: No. 360, Sec. 3, Yimin Rd., Xinpu Township, Hsinchu County
description: Most temples worship a statue. The Yimin Temple worships a grave — and that is what makes Baozhong Yimin Temple so unusual, and so moving. Standing in Xinpu Township, Hsinchu County, it is the head temple of Yimin faith in Taiwan and the most important spiritual site of Taiwan's Hakka people. The heart of its faith is the Yimin Tomb behind the temple, resting place of the Hakka volunteers who died defending their homes in Qing-era upheavals such as the Lin Shuangwen Incident. The "Baozhong" plaque hanging high in the main hall bears two characters bestowed by Emperor Qianlong himself. The Yimin Festival on the 20th day of the 7th lunar month is hosted in rotation by fifteen great villages of the Taoyuan–Hsinchu region, and its best-loved event is the "Divine Pig Competition" — devotees vie to raise the fattest offering pig, honoring their forebears in the most generous way they know.
history: In 1786 (the 51st year of the Qianlong reign), the Lin Shuangwen Incident broke out, and Hakka villagers around Hsinchu and Taoyuan formed volunteer forces and fought to defend their homes. After the fighting, the fallen were buried together at Fangliao (today's Xinpu). In 1788 (the 53rd year of Qianlong), the villagers began pooling money to build a memorial temple; the main hall was completed in 1790, and Emperor Qianlong bestowed the "Baozhong" plaque — and so the Yimin Temple came to be. Volunteers who died in the Dai Chaochun Incident during the Tongzhi era were later buried in an annex grave beside the Yimin Tomb. In this way the temple became the sacred symbol of the Taiwanese Hakka spirit, and its unique form of faith — a tomb at the center of a temple — has always stood apart in Taiwan's religious culture.

name: Xinzhuang Wu Temple
address: No. 340, Xinzhuang Rd, Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City
description: Other temples paint fierce door gods on their gates; the gate panels of Xinzhuang Wu Temple are bare, studded only with 108 door nails — symbols of the Thirty-Six Heavenly Generals and Seventy-Two Earthly Fiends, meaning that Guansheng Dijun's martial prowess is so supreme he needs no door gods to guard him. This temple in Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City, is the oldest Guan Di temple in northern Taiwan and a designated historic site. It witnessed the prosperous era of Xinzhuang's 'forest of a thousand sails' as a port, and to this day preserves many precious old plaques and stele inscriptions, an important relic for the study of Xinzhuang's history.
history: During the Yongzheng reign (around the 1730s), immigrants from Zhangzhou, Fujian, pooled their funds to build Wu Temple, dedicated to the God of War, Lord Guan. Xinzhuang was then the most flourishing port and trading town in northern Taiwan, its harbor crowded with masts and sails, and Wu Temple was where the merchants prayed for thriving business and urged one another toward loyalty and honesty. It was renovated and expanded many times through the Qianlong and Jiaqing reigns, and in the Daoguang era it received an official inscribed plaque, formally becoming a temple of the officially recognized sacrificial register. Under Japanese rule this old temple once faced the threat of demolition, and survived only through the determined protection of local gentry. It still holds precious relics — Qing-dynasty stelae, old plaques, and stone lions — quietly witnessing Xinzhuang's century of change from a thriving port to a modern town.

name: Xinzhuang Dizang An
address: No. 84, Zhongzheng Rd, Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City
description: Those fierce, elaborately face-painted 'Guan Jiang Shou' (Officers of the Vanguard) seen at Taiwanese temple festivals originated right here at Xinzhuang Dizang An. This temple in Xinzhuang District, New Taipei City — commonly called the 'Dazhong Temple' — is dedicated to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva and Wen-Wu Dazhong Ye, presiding over the finding of lost items, the settling of lawsuits, and the driving out of evil, and is a vital center of faith in the Xinzhuang area. On the 1st day of the 5th lunar month each year, the 'Great Xinzhuang Worship' (the Dazhong Ye procession), with its distinctive 'night patrol' rite paired with Guan Jiang Shou performance troupes, is one of the most representative temple festivals in northern Taiwan — well worth a special trip to feel that atmosphere at once fearsome and festive.
history: Dizang An was completed in Xinzhuang during the Qianlong reign (around 1757), one of the oldest Ksitigarbha temples in northern Taiwan. Xinzhuang was in its early days an important commercial port in the north, densely populated but often visited by plague and disaster, and Dizang An became a vital place to deliver wandering souls and pray for the community's peace. The Zhongyuan (Ghost Festival) rites of the 7th lunar month are the temple's grandest moment, with the 'Wen-Wu Dazhong Ye procession' and the 'Guan Jiang Shou' troupe performance the most famous — for Xinzhuang is the very birthplace of the Guan Jiang Shou tradition, those fierce-faced officers charged with awing demons and keeping order between the worlds of the living and the dead, now designated an intangible cultural asset of New Taipei City.

name: Xinzhuang Guangfu Temple
address: No. 150, Xinzhuang Rd., Xinzhuang Dist., New Taipei City
description: Of the four old temples on Xinzhuang's old street, the best preserved is, oddly, the one that lost its worshippers: Guangfu Temple, which locals still call the Three Mountain Kings Temple. The Three Mountain Kings are a local faith from Chaozhou in Guangdong, carried across the strait by Chaozhou settlers. When those settlers later left Xinzhuang, the temple lost its incense and its patrons — and so escaped the rounds of renovation that remade its neighbors, keeping its Qing-dynasty face. Today it is a national monument: the gate carvings are cut from Guanyin Mountain stone, the roof frame is Minnan-style yet uses rare square beams, and the front is built of red brick while the rear is dark brick. Slow down here when you walk the old street.
history: Guangfu Temple was built in 1780, the 45th year of the Qianlong reign, with money from Xinzhuang's Chaozhou immigrants from Guangdong, and dedicated to the Three Mountain Kings. A great fire destroyed it in 1882. In 1888, Hsinchu gentleman Chen Chao-gang rallied people from the nine Chaozhou counties to rebuild it — and the rebuilt temple was left unpainted, a plain look it still keeps today. It was repaired again in 1936. In 1985 it was designated a second-grade historic site (now a national monument), and restoration work ran from 1991 to 1995.

name: Hsinchu Putian Temple
address: No. 66, Ln. 306, Gaofeng Rd., East Dist., Hsinchu City
description: Before you even reach Hsinchu Putian Temple, you'll first catch sight of the towering statue of Guansheng Dijun (Lord Guan) rising 120 meters high — grand and imposing, visible from far off, the temple's most famous landmark. This temple in Hsinchu's East District is dedicated to Guansheng Dijun, and being near the Hsinchu Science Park, it is a center of faith for many of the park's tech workers. Beyond Lord Guan, Putian Temple's Matchmaker (Yue Lao) is also well known, drawing many single men and women to pray for a good match — seeking a little guidance for their love lives in this efficiency-driven tech city.
history: Hsinchu Putian Temple was founded during the Daoguang reign of the Qing dynasty (around the 1840s), built with funds raised by Hakka devotees of the Hsinchu area, at first only a small temple. It was renovated and expanded many times thereafter, gradually growing to its present scale. Under Japanese rule the temple was once requisitioned, and was restored by local devotees only after the war. Its architecture is plain yet solemn, and it still preserves some Qing-dynasty stone-carved components. Over the years the temple has continued to run community services and lectures, keeping close ties with the surrounding neighborhood — an important place in the Hsinchu area that serves both religious faith and community cohesion.

name: Sanxia Changfu Temple
address: No. 1, Changfu St, Sanxia District, New Taipei City
description: Walk into Sanxia Changfu Temple and don't look up at the statues first — look at the pillars. The birds, flowers, and figures on every stone column were cut by hand, deep enough to slip a finger into. This temple to Qingshui Zushi has been rebuilt since 1947 under the direction of Li Mei-shu, a painter born in Sanxia, who brought the training of Western fine art into a traditional temple and kept at it for decades. He died before the work was finished. That is why Changfu Temple is that rare thing in Taiwan: an old temple still being built, a relay across three generations of craftsmen. It was designated a New Taipei City heritage site in 2018.
history: In 1767, Anxi migrants from Quanzhou settled around Sanxia, Yingge, Shulin, and Daxi and proposed a temple; it was completed two years later, in 1769, enshrining the Qingshui Zushi of their home region. The area was then called Sanjiaoyong, where three rivers meet, and the temple stood at the center of the settlement — a place of worship and a place where migrants settled their affairs. Its transformation came in the twentieth century. In 1947 the painter Li Mei-shu took charge of the rebuilding. He refused to rush; every carving had to be worthy of the temple, and the work stretched across decades. The layered stonework you see today is what that patience left behind.

name: Manka Qingshui Temple
address: No. 81, Kangding Rd, Wanhua District, Taipei City
description: Manka Qingshui Temple is one of the few old temples in Taipei that is only half there. It once had three halls; the rear hall burned in a communal fight and was never rebuilt, so the building simply stops — and that absence became part of its history. Known locally as the Zushi Temple, it enshrines Qingshui Zushi and was funded by Anxi migrants in 1787. It ranks with Longshan Temple and Baoan Temple as one of the "three great temple gates of Taipei," and is a designated city heritage site. Inside it is quieter than you expect: none of Longshan's crowds, light falling through the courtyard, dark timber absorbing half the sound. If you want somewhere in Wanhua to sit for a while, this beats the streets around it.
history: In 1787, Anxi migrants chose Weng You-lai as director and raised thirty thousand silver dollars to build the temple; it was completed in 1790, enshrining a Qingshui Zushi image brought from the original Qingshui Temple in their home county. What changed the temple's fate came in 1853, when fighting broke out in Manka between migrant groups. Fire reached the temple and destroyed it. Believers rebuilt in 1867, but the rear hall was never restored. That unrepaired gap is now the most direct evidence of how Taipei's earliest commercial district grew: out of conflict, and out of rebuilding.

name: Tamsui Qingshui Temple
address: No. 87, Qingshui St, Tamsui District, New Taipei City
description: The Qingshui Zushi enshrined in Tamsui goes by the most vivid name in Taiwan: the Nose-Dropping Ancestor. Legend says that when disaster approaches, the nose of the statue falls off as a warning. It sounds absurd until you hear a Tamsui local tell it — they are entirely serious, because the story is about the survival of a whole town. Built in 1937, the temple is young by local standards, yet it counts among greater Taipei's four great Zushi temples and Tamsui's four great temples. It sits inside the market lanes off Qingshui Street: turn in from the crowded old street and within a few steps the noise gives way to incense smoke. In Tamsui, the busiest and the stillest are one corner apart.
history: Tamsui Qingshui Temple was built in 1937, late compared with other Zushi temples in Taiwan — but the deity it enshrines had been part of Tamsui life far longer than the building. The story of the falling nose circulated in the neighborhood before there was any temple, and believers took turns hosting the image in private homes until the hall was finished and it finally had a fixed address. That sequence — faith first, temple after — is why this place is bound so tightly to the streets around it. Nobody built a temple and waited for worshippers; people believed for decades, then built the temple together. It is now counted among the four great Zushi temples of greater Taipei, alongside those of Manka, Sanxia, and Ruifang.

name: Tamsui Yinshan Temple
address: No. 15, Denggong Rd, Tamsui District, New Taipei City
description: Yinshan Temple will make you rethink what a temple is: the side chambers here were not built for a deity, but for people to sleep in. Founded in 1822 by Hakka migrants from Tingzhou in western Fujian, it enshrines their guardian, Dingguang Gufo, and set aside its two wings as the Tingzhou Guild Hall so that newcomers from home had somewhere to stay the moment they stepped off the boat. Only two Qing-era Dingguang Buddha temples survive in Taiwan; this is the northern one, and the better preserved — two halls, two corridors, two side chambers, now a national heritage site. For those migrants the building was at once the god's home and their own: settle the faith first, then settle the body.
history: In 1822, Hakka migrants from the eight counties of Tingzhou prefecture in western Fujian built Yinshan Temple in Tamsui. They were a relative minority among Taiwan's settlers — different in speech, in origin, and in custom from the Quanzhou and Zhangzhou communities around them — so from the beginning the temple was more than a place of worship. Its side chambers served as the Tingzhou Guild Hall, lodging for countrymen who had just crossed the strait and had nowhere yet to go. The deity in the main hall, the newcomers in the wings: one building taking the word "protection" literally. The layout has barely changed in two hundred years, which is why it stands today as a national heritage site and the best preserved Dingguang Buddha temple in Taiwan.

name: Linkou Zhulinshan Guanyin Temple
address: No. 325, Zhulin Rd, Linkou District, New Taipei City
description: The temple's name is assembled from three places — Luzhu, Linkou, and Guishan, one character each. The naming is honest about what this is: not one village's temple, but a center of faith raised by three communities together. It enshrines the eighteen-armed Guanyin, and the halls completed in the 2012 rebuild used thirty-eight thousand-year-old Taiwanese cypress timbers; what you notice first on entering is the smell of wood, not incense. Outside lies a garden of several hectares, cherry blossoms in spring, and on a weekday morning close to nothing but the sound of someone sweeping — one of the few places near Taipei that manages to be both large and quiet.
history: In 1801, worshippers brought three Guanyin images from the Longshan Temple of Anhai, Jinjiang, in Fujian. At first there was no temple; households across the villages took turns hosting the images. The real test came late in the Japanese colonial period, when the assimilation campaign suppressed Taiwanese folk religion and sought to burn its statues — believers hid the Guanyin and kept worship going in secret. The colonial government eventually permitted a temple in Japanese style, completed at the present site in 1939, and the name was made from one character each of Luzhu, Linkou, and Guishan to record who had protected it together. After study trips abroad, the temple completed its current rebuild in 2012.

name: Manka Dizang Temple
address: No. 245, Xichang St, Wanhua District, Taipei City
description: Manka Dizang Temple is small enough to walk straight past — a single hall three bays wide, wedged between shopfronts on Xichang Street, with no archway and no forecourt. That is precisely what makes it valuable. Most of Taipei's old temples expanded over two centuries; this one kept the form of a mid-Qing single-hall temple, swallowtail ridge, gable walls, and rolled-roof entrance corridor intact. It enshrines Ksitigarbha, with Marshal Tian Du and the City God in attendance. It is not a tourist stop; most days there are only a few old neighbors sitting by the door. If you want to see what a temple originally looked like rather than what restoration made of it, this is Taipei's plainest example.
history: Manka Dizang Temple was built in 1760 and repaired in 1838, making it one of the earliest surviving temples in Taipei. It faced a crisis under Japanese rule, when the authorities moved to bring folk temples into public ownership; to keep the property, the temple transferred management to Manka Longshan Temple, and that arrangement carried it through. Because it was never substantially rebuilt, it preserves the full form of a mid-Qing single-hall temple and is now a designated heritage site. Each year on the thirtieth day of the seventh lunar month, Ksitigarbha's feast day, this quiet little temple holds a large universal deliverance rite — its busiest day of the year, and the way Wanhua remembers it.

name: Xinpu Guanghe Temple
address: No. 608, Zhongzheng Rd., Xinpu Township, Hsinchu County
description: In 1895, during the Japanese invasion of Taiwan, Japanese troops set fire to Xinpu's main street, and Guanghe Temple's front hall, middle hall and statues all burned. The temple you see today was rebuilt piece by piece afterward: first a simple middle hall of mud brick in 1902, then nearly ten years of major renovation starting in 1919. Xinpu Guanghe Temple is dedicated to the Three Mountain Kings — locals also call it the Wangye Temple — a hometown faith carried here by Xinpu's Chaozhou settlers. That renovation left fine koji pottery, including a piece signed by the Quanzhou master Su Yang-shui in 1928. Xinpu is known for its old street and Hakka ancestral halls; stop by while you walk the old street.
history: Guanghe Temple was founded during the Xianfeng reign of the Qing dynasty. Xinpu was then called Baligui, and Chaozhou settlers built the temple to honor the Three Mountain Kings of their homeland, at the call of local gentleman Pan Rong-guang. In 1859 the temple walls had collapsed, so Pan Rong-guang, Cai Liang-zhen, Chen Chao-gang and others raised funds for repairs, finished the following year (1860). In 1895 Japanese troops burned Xinpu's main street, destroying the front and middle halls and the statues. In 1902 Pan Cheng-yuan funded a simple middle hall of mud brick, and Fuzhou craftsmen Lin Fa-ben and Lin Qi-feng sculpted new statues of the Three Mountain Kings and other deities — twelve in all. From 1919, local gentry funded a major renovation that took about ten years, completed and consecrated in 1928. During the Japanese assimilation campaign in 1940, statues from nearby temples were moved here, and the temple renamed itself "Huiming Temple" to get by.
